Higher Criticism
HY-er KRIT-i-sizm
noun phrase (academic method)
Term coined in late-18th-century German biblical scholarship to distinguish "lower" or textual criticism (manuscript-collation; legitimate work) from "higher" criticism (questions of authorship, date, sources, composition; the academic method the dictionary rebuts). The term höhere Kritik is associated with Johann Eichhorn (1780s).

Biblical Definition

Higher criticism is the academic method that approaches the biblical text with the working assumption that its claims about authorship, date, sources, composition, and historicity may be revised on naturalistic-historical grounds against the canonical claims. Originating in the German Aufklärung (Enlightenment) of the late 18th century — Eichhorn, Reimarus, Lessing, then de Wette, F.C. Baur, Wellhausen, Bultmann — it produced the now-standard academic theories that the Reformed-confessional reader rejects: documentary hypothesis (JEDP) for the Pentateuch, denying Mosaic authorship; multiple-Isaiah theory; late dating of Daniel (second century BC after the prophesied events); rejection of Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles; mythological-versus-historical readings of the Gospels; the quest of the historical Jesus that denies the supernatural elements of the canonical record. The method's defining move is that the canonical text's self-witness about itself (Moses wrote, Isaiah wrote, Daniel wrote, Paul wrote) is replaced by the modern academic reconstruction. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the canonical self-witness is authoritative because the canonical text is the inspired Word of God (2 Tim 3:16); the academic-critical reconstruction is human conjecture against divine testimony. The dictionary's authorship convictions (single Isaiah; sixth-century Daniel; Pauline authorship of all 13 epistles; Mosaic Pentateuch; apostolic Gospels) are the historic Christian position from the apostolic age through Calvin and the Reformers, and are held against the higher-critical reconstruction. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts higher criticism by name.

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-18th-century German academic method approaching the biblical text with naturalistic-historical assumptions against canonical claims; produces JEDP, multiple-Isaiah, late-Daniel, deutero-Pauline theories; rebutted from canonical self-witness + 2 Tim 3:16 inspired-Word doctrine.

HIGHER CRITICISM, noun phrase. German Aufklärung biblical method, late 18th century onward.

Distinct from textual / lower criticism (legitimate manuscript-collation work that the dictionary affirms).

Major theorists: Eichhorn (1780s); Reimarus and Lessing; de Wette; F.C. Baur (Tübingen school); Julius Wellhausen (documentary hypothesis, 1878); Rudolf Bultmann (form criticism, demythologization).

Major outputs: JEDP documentary hypothesis; multiple-Isaiah theory; second-century-BC Daniel; deutero-Pauline Pastoral Epistles; quest of the historical Jesus.

Rebutted from canonical self-witness + verbal-plenary inspiration of Scripture (2 Tim 3:16; 2 Pet 1:21).

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16-17 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works."

2 Peter 1:20-21 — "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

Matthew 5:17-18 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

John 10:35 — "If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken."

Modern Corruption

Higher criticism is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry exists to identify the method, name its representatives, document its standard outputs, and rebut it from the canonical self-witness plus the verbal-plenary inspiration of Scripture.

expand to see more

Naturalistic assumption against canonical self-witness. Higher criticism's defining move is the methodological commitment that the biblical text's claims about itself must be evaluated by naturalistic-historical reconstruction rather than received as authoritative. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal: the canonical self-witness IS the data; the academic reconstruction is the conjecture. Moses wrote the Pentateuch because the Pentateuch (and the Lord Jesus at Mark 12:26, John 5:46-47, Luke 24:44) says he did. Isaiah wrote Isaiah because Isaiah and the Lord Jesus (Matt 13:14-15 citing Isa 6, etc.) say he did. The methodological assumption that the text's self-witness must yield to academic reconstruction is the corruption pattern. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this paragraph rebuts the higher-critical methodological assumption.

Wellhausen's documentary hypothesis specifically. The most famous higher-critical product, Julius Wellhausen's 1878 reconstruction of the Pentateuch as four post-Mosaic sources (J, E, D, P), was decisively criticized within secular academic Old Testament studies in the late 20th century (the work of Whybray, Rendtorff, the so-called 'collapse of the documentary hypothesis' in the 1980s-2000s), and continues to be defended only in soft / minimalist forms. The Reformed-confessional reader notes both that the historic Christian position (Mosaic authorship) was right all along, and that secular academic biblical studies' own internal criticism eventually corroborated this from the inside. Higher criticism's confidence in its own results has been chastened by its own intra-disciplinary history.

Origin: late-18th-century German Aufklärung; term höhere Kritik from Johann Eichhorn (1780s)

Major theorists: Eichhorn; Reimarus; Lessing; de Wette; F.C. Baur and the Tübingen school; Julius Wellhausen (Prolegomena, 1878); Rudolf Bultmann (form criticism, demythologization)

Major outputs: JEDP documentary hypothesis; multiple-Isaiah; late-Daniel; deutero-Pauline Pastorals; quest of the historical Jesus

Reformed-confessional rebuttals: B.B. Warfield (The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible); R. Laird Harris; E.J. Young (An Introduction to the Old Testament); G.K. Beale; Iain Provan

Distinct from textual / lower criticism, which the dictionary affirms

Usage

"Higher criticism — the late-18th-century German academic method that approaches the biblical text against its own self-witness."

"All scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Tim 3:16) — the apostolic axiom that the higher-critical method denies in principle and the dictionary affirms."

"Distinguished from textual / lower criticism, which the dictionary affirms as legitimate manuscript-collation work."
